solution:
Atoms placed side by side in a line occupy one atomic DIAMETER each.

Diameter \(= 0.15\,\text{nm} = 1.5 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\); length of scale \(= 20\,\text{cm} = 0.20\,\text{m}\).

\(n = \dfrac{0.20\,\text{m}}{1.5 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}} = 1.33 \times 10^{9}\)

Answer: \(1.33 \times 10^{9}\) carbon atoms.

The total length is the number of atoms times one atomic diameter.

\(d = \dfrac{2.4\,\text{cm}}{2 \times 10^{8}} = \dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}}{2 \times 10^{8}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\)

Radius \(= \dfrac{d}{2} = 6.0 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: \(r = 6.0 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m} = 0.06\,\text{nm} = 60\,\text{pm}\).

\(d = 2.6\,\text{Å} = 2.6 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m} = 260\,\text{pm}\).

(a) Radius \(= \dfrac{260\,\text{pm}}{2} = 130\,\text{pm}\)

(b) Atoms arranged lengthwise occupy one diameter each, so over \(1.6\,\text{cm} = 1.6 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\):

\(n = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}}{2.6 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}} = 6.15 \times 10^{7}\)

Answer: (a) \(130\,\text{pm}\); (b) \(6.15 \times 10^{7}\) atoms.

Charge is quantised in units of the electronic charge, \(e = 1.6022 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\).

\(n = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-16}\,\text{C}}{1.6022 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 1560\)

Answer: \(1.56 \times 10^{3}\) electrons (1560).

The magnitude of the charge on the drop must be a whole-number multiple of \(e\) (this quantisation is exactly what Millikan's experiment established).

\(n = \dfrac{1.282 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{C}}{1.6022 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 8.00\)

Answer: 8 electrons.

In the notation \(^{A}_{Z}\text{X}\) the SUPERSCRIPT is the mass number \(A\) and the SUBSCRIPT is the atomic number \(Z\). The two are not interchangeable, and they play different roles:

- \(Z\) is fixed by the element symbol itself — bromine is \(Z = 35\) whatever isotope is meant — so \(Z\) is redundant information and may be omitted. That is why both \(^{79}_{35}\text{Br}\) and \(^{79}\text{Br}\) are acceptable.
- \(A\) is NOT fixed by the symbol, because isotopes of one element differ in \(A\). It therefore cannot be dropped.

So \(^{35}_{79}\text{Br}\) is unacceptable because the two numbers have been interchanged: it claims \(Z = 79\) for bromine (wrong element) and \(A = 35\), which is smaller than \(Z\) and would need a negative number of neutrons.

And \(^{35}\text{Br}\) is unacceptable because a lone superscript reads as the MASS number; \(A = 35\) for bromine would mean \(35 - 35 = 0\) neutrons, which no bromine nucleus has. The 35 intended here is the atomic number, and the atomic number is exactly the one that must not be written in the superscript position.

Let the number of protons be \(Z\). Then the number of neutrons is \(31.7\%\) greater:

neutrons \(= Z + 0.317Z = 1.317Z\)

Mass number \(A = \text{protons} + \text{neutrons}\):

\(Z + 1.317Z = 81\)

\(2.317Z = 81 \Rightarrow Z = 34.96 \approx 35\)

\(Z = 35\) is bromine, and neutrons \(= 81 - 35 = 46\) (check: \(46/35 = 1.314\), i.e. \(31.4\%\) more, consistent to the precision given).

Answer: \(^{81}_{35}\text{Br}\).

The ion carries one unit of NEGATIVE charge, so it has one electron more than protons:

electrons \(= Z + 1\), neutrons \(= A - Z = 37 - Z\)

The neutrons exceed the electrons by \(11.1\%\):

\(37 - Z = 1.111(Z + 1)\)

\(37 - Z = 1.111Z + 1.111\)

\(35.889 = 2.111Z \Rightarrow Z = 17.0\)

\(Z = 17\) is chlorine; electrons \(= 18\), neutrons \(= 37 - 17 = 20\) (check: \(20/18 = 1.111\)).

Answer: \(^{37}_{17}\text{Cl}^{-}\).

The ion carries three units of POSITIVE charge, so it has three electrons fewer than protons:

electrons \(= Z - 3\), neutrons \(= A - Z = 56 - Z\)

The neutrons exceed the electrons by \(30.4\%\):

\(56 - Z = 1.304(Z - 3)\)

\(56 - Z = 1.304Z - 3.912\)

\(59.912 = 2.304Z \Rightarrow Z = 26.0\)

\(Z = 26\) is iron; electrons \(= 23\), neutrons \(= 56 - 26 = 30\) (check: \(30/23 = 1.304\)).

Answer: \(^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}^{3+}\).

[Textbook answer-key error in the DIRECTION of the ordering. The question asks for the species arranged in order of INCREASING size, and the key prints its list in DECREASING order. The sequence of species the key names is right; it is the stated direction that is reversed, so a reader comparing answers should compare the two lists end-to-end rather than term-by-term.] Frequency increases as wavelength decreases (\(\nu = c/\lambda\)). Placing the five sources on the electromagnetic spectrum:

- FM radio: radiowaves, \(\lambda \sim\) metres — lowest frequency
- microwave oven: microwaves, \(\lambda \sim\) centimetres
- amber traffic light: visible, \(\lambda \sim 600\,\text{nm}\)
- X-rays: \(\lambda \sim 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\)
- cosmic rays: shortest wavelength of all — highest frequency

Answer, in increasing order of frequency: (c) radiation from FM radio \(<\) (a) radiation from microwave oven \(<\) (b) amber light from traffic signal \(<\) (e) X-rays \(<\) (d) cosmic rays from outer space.

Energy of one photon at \(\lambda = 337.1\,\text{nm}\):

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}{337.1 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 5.897 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

Total energy emitted by \(5.6 \times 10^{24}\) photons:

\(E_{\text{total}} = (5.897 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J})(5.6 \times 10^{24}) = 3.30 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J}\)

Answer: \(3.30 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J}\).
_note: The stem asks for the 'power' of the laser, but gives no time over which the photons are emitted, and power = energy/time. The quantity that the data actually determines is the total ENERGY emitted, 3.30 x 10^6 J; it is a power only if the emission is taken to occur in one second.

solution:
\(\lambda = 616\,\text{nm} = 616 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}\).

(a) \(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{616 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 4.87 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

(b) Light travels at \(c\) whatever its wavelength:

distance \(= (3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1})(30\,\text{s}) = 9.0 \times 10^{9}\,\text{m}\)

(c) \(E = h\nu = (6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(4.87 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}) = 3.23 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

(d) \(n = \dfrac{2\,\text{J}}{3.23 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 6.20 \times 10^{18}\)

Answer: (a) \(4.87 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\); (b) \(9.0 \times 10^{9}\,\text{m}\); (c) \(3.23 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\); (d) \(6.20 \times 10^{18}\) quanta.

Energy of one 600 nm photon:

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{600 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.313 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

Number of photons in \(3.15 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}\):

\(n = \dfrac{3.15 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}}{3.313 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 9.51\)

Since photons are indivisible, the detector received about 10 photons.

Answer: \(n \approx 9.51\), i.e. approximately 10 photons.

The only time given is the 2 ns pulse duration, so take the frequency of the radiation as the reciprocal of that duration:

\(\nu = \dfrac{1}{2 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{s}} = 5 \times 10^{8}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

Energy of one photon:

\(E = h\nu = (6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(5 \times 10^{8}\,\text{s}^{-1}) = 3.313 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\)

Energy of the source, for \(2.5 \times 10^{15}\) photons:

\(E_{\text{total}} = (3.313 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{J})(2.5 \times 10^{15}) = 8.28 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{J}\)

Answer: \(8.28 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{J}\).
_note: The stem gives no wavelength or frequency for the radiation itself, so the frequency has been taken as the reciprocal of the stated 2 ns pulse duration. That assumption is stated explicitly because it is the only route from the given data to an energy.

solution:
\(\nu = c/\lambda\) for each line of the doublet.

\(\nu_1 = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{589 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 5.0934 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

\(\nu_2 = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{589.6 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 5.0882 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

The two absorptions start from the same lower level, so the energy difference between the two excited states is

\(\Delta E = h(\nu_1 - \nu_2) = (6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(5.18 \times 10^{11}\,\text{s}^{-1})\)

\(= 3.43 \times 10^{-22}\,\text{J}\)

Answer: \(\nu_1 = 5.093 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\), \(\nu_2 = 5.088 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\); \(\Delta E = 3.43 \times 10^{-22}\,\text{J}\).

\(W_0 = 1.9\,\text{eV} = (1.9)(1.602 \times 10^{-19}) = 3.044 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\).

(a) At the threshold the whole photon energy is used to free the electron:

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W_0} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{3.044 \times 10^{-19}} = 6.53 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 653\,\text{nm}\)

(b) \(\nu_0 = \dfrac{c}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{6.53 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.59 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

With \(\lambda = 500\,\text{nm}\):

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 3.976 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

Kinetic energy \(= E - W_0 = 3.976 \times 10^{-19} - 3.044 \times 10^{-19} = 9.32 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J}\)

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 9.32 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}}} = 4.52 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Answer: (a) \(\lambda_0 = 653\,\text{nm}\); (b) \(\nu_0 = 4.59 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\); K.E. \(= 9.32 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J}\) (\(0.58\,\text{eV}\)); \(v = 4.52 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

[Textbook errors — TWO, and the second means the question has no single right answer. (1) UNIT: the table heads the velocities \(\text{cm s}^{-1}\); they must be read as \(\text{m s}^{-1}\), or Planck's constant comes out near \(10^{-38}\), four orders of magnitude from its accepted value. (2) THE DATA ARE NOT SELF-CONSISTENT. Einstein's photoelectric equation makes kinetic energy linear in \(1/\lambda\), so the three \((\lambda, v)\) points should be collinear and they are not — the answer therefore depends entirely on which PAIR of rows you use: 500 and 450 nm give \(h = 8.49 \times 10^{-34}\) and \(\lambda_0 = 531\,\text{nm}\); 500 and 400 nm give \(h = 6.72 \times 10^{-34}\) and \(\lambda_0 = 540\,\text{nm}\); 450 and 400 nm give \(h = 5.30 \times 10^{-34}\) and \(\lambda_0 = 595\,\text{nm}\). The printed key's \(530.9\,\text{nm}\) reproduces the 500/450 pairing exactly — but that pairing implies a Planck's constant 28% above the accepted \(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\), which is precisely the quantity part (b) asks the student to determine, and the key prints no value of \(h\) at all, so its own inconsistency never surfaces. The answer below uses the 500/400 pairing, which returns \(h = 6.72 \times 10^{-34}\), within 1.4% of the accepted value; a least-squares fit to all three points gives \(h = 6.66 \times 10^{-34}\) and \(\lambda_0 \approx 546\,\text{nm}\). Expect \(531\,\text{nm}\) in any answer key.] Einstein's equation gives \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = W_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}m_e v^2\). Subtracting the equation for one wavelength from that for another eliminates \(W_0\) and leaves \(h\).

The velocities are \(v_1 = 2.55 \times 10^{5}\), \(v_2 = 4.35 \times 10^{5}\), \(v_3 = 5.35 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

Kinetic energies (\(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}\)):

\(\text{K.E.}_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.11 \times 10^{-31})(2.55 \times 10^{5})^2 = 2.962 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J}\)

\(\text{K.E.}_3 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.11 \times 10^{-31})(5.35 \times 10^{5})^2 = 1.304 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

(b) Using the 500 nm and 400 nm rows,

\(hc\left[\dfrac{1}{\lambda_3} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_1}\right] = \text{K.E.}_3 - \text{K.E.}_1\)

\(h(3 \times 10^{8})\left[\dfrac{1}{400 \times 10^{-9}} - \dfrac{1}{500 \times 10^{-9}}\right] = 1.008 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(h(3 \times 10^{8})(5.0 \times 10^{5}) = 1.008 \times 10^{-19}\)

\(h = 6.72 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\)

(a) Substituting back into the 500 nm row,

\(W_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} - \text{K.E.}_1 = 4.030 \times 10^{-19} - 2.962 \times 10^{-20} = 3.734 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W_0} = \dfrac{2.015 \times 10^{-25}}{3.734 \times 10^{-19}} = 5.40 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: (a) threshold wavelength \(\lambda_0 \approx 540\,\text{nm}\); (b) \(h \approx 6.72 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\) (close to the accepted \(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\)).
_note: The table's unit is printed as 'v x 10^-5 (cm s^-1)', which would give v = 2.55 x 10^3 m/s and yields h ~ 6.7 x 10^-38 J s — four orders of magnitude wrong. Reading the unit as m s^-1 (so v = 2.55 x 10^5 m s^-1) reproduces h = 6.7 x 10^-34 J s, so the printed 'cm' appears to be a misprint for 'm'. Solved on the metre reading; flagged for the cross-check to adjudicate.

solution:
The stopping potential \(V_0\) measures the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons: \(\text{K.E.}_{\max} = eV_0\), i.e. \(0.35\,\text{eV}\).

Energy of the incident photon:

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{256.7 \times 10^{-9}} = 7.744 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(= \dfrac{7.744 \times 10^{-19}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} = 4.83\,\text{eV}\)

From \(h\nu = W_0 + \text{K.E.}_{\max}\):

\(W_0 = 4.83 - 0.35 = 4.48\,\text{eV}\)

Answer: \(W_0 = 4.48\,\text{eV} = 7.18 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\).

The photon's energy is shared between the binding energy of the electron and the kinetic energy it carries away:

\(E_{\text{photon}} = E_{\text{binding}} + \text{K.E.}\)

\(E_{\text{photon}} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{150 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{m}} = 1.325 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{J}\)

\(\text{K.E.} = \tfrac{1}{2}m_e v^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg})(1.5 \times 10^{7}\,\text{m s}^{-1})^2 = 1.025 \times 10^{-16}\,\text{J}\)

\(E_{\text{binding}} = 1.325 \times 10^{-15} - 1.025 \times 10^{-16} = 1.223 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{J}\)

Answer: \(1.22 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{J}\) (about \(7.6\,\text{keV}\)).

Convert the observed wavelength to a frequency:

\(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{1285 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 2.335 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

Substitute into the given expression:

\(2.335 \times 10^{14} = 3.29 \times 10^{15}\left[\dfrac{1}{3^2} - \dfrac{1}{n^2}\right]\)

\(\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{2.335 \times 10^{14}}{3.29 \times 10^{15}} = 0.07096\)

\(\dfrac{1}{n^2} = 0.11111 - 0.07096 = 0.04015\)

\(n^2 = 24.9 \Rightarrow n = 4.99 \approx 5\)

Answer: \(n = 5\). The Paschen series ends at \(n = 3\) and lies in the INFRARED region of the spectrum.

For hydrogen \(r_n = (0.0529\,\text{nm})n^2\), so each radius identifies its level.

Start: \(n^2 = \dfrac{1.3225\,\text{nm}}{0.0529\,\text{nm}} = 25 \Rightarrow n_i = 5\)

End: \(211.6\,\text{pm} = 0.2116\,\text{nm}\), so \(n^2 = \dfrac{0.2116}{0.0529} = 4 \Rightarrow n_f = 2\)

\(\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left[\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{25}\right] = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}(0.21) = 4.578 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{4.578 \times 10^{-19}} = 4.34 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: \(\lambda = 434\,\text{nm}\); the transition \(n = 5 \rightarrow n = 2\) belongs to the BALMER series and lies in the VISIBLE region.

de Broglie relation \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m v}\), with \(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}\).

\(\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}{(9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg})(1.6 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1})} = 4.55 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: \(\lambda = 4.55 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\) (\(455\,\text{pm}\), i.e. \(0.455\,\text{nm}\)).

Rearrange the de Broglie relation for the velocity, using the neutron mass \(m_n = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}\) and \(\lambda = 800\,\text{pm} = 8.0 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\):

\(v = \dfrac{h}{m_n \lambda} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}{(1.675 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg})(8.0 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m})}\)

\(= \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{1.34 \times 10^{-36}} = 494.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Answer: \(v = 4.95 \times 10^{2}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_e v} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}{(9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg})(2.19 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}\)

\(= \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{1.995 \times 10^{-24}} = 3.32 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: \(\lambda = 3.32 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\) (\(332\,\text{pm}\)). This equals \(2\pi r_1\) for the first Bohr orbit (\(r_1 = 52.9\,\text{pm}\)), as the standing-wave condition \(2\pi r = n\lambda\) with \(n = 1\) requires.

Apply the de Broglie relation to the hockey ball, taking the stated velocity \(v = 4.37 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and mass \(m = 0.1\,\text{kg}\):

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m v} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}{(0.1\,\text{kg})(4.37 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}\)

\(= \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{4.37 \times 10^{4}} = 1.52 \times 10^{-38}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: \(\lambda = 1.52 \times 10^{-38}\,\text{m}\) — utterly undetectable, which is why the wave nature of ordinary objects is never observed.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: \(\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \dfrac{h}{4\pi}\).

With \(\Delta x = 0.002\,\text{nm} = 2 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{m}\):

\(\Delta p = \dfrac{h}{4\pi \Delta x} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}{4 \times 3.1416 \times 2 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{m}} = 2.64 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)

For the second part, evaluate the stated momentum \(\dfrac{h}{4\pi \times 0.05\,\text{nm}}\):

\(p = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{4 \times 3.1416 \times 5 \times 10^{-11}} = 1.05 \times 10^{-24}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)

YES, there is a problem: this momentum is about 25 times SMALLER than the uncertainty \(\Delta p\) just calculated. The uncertainty in a quantity cannot exceed the quantity itself — a momentum quoted to a precision far finer than its own value is meaningless, so that value cannot be defined for an electron localised to \(\pm 0.002\,\text{nm}\).

Answer: \(\Delta p = 2.64 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\); and yes — since the stated momentum \((1.05 \times 10^{-24}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1})\) is smaller than its own uncertainty, it cannot be meaningfully defined.
_note: The printed expression reads 'h/4π_m x 0.05 nm' with an 'm' subscripted to pi. Read here as h/(4π x 0.05 nm), which is the only form that yields a quantity with the dimensions of momentum and makes the comparison the question invites.

solution:
Orbital energies follow the \((n + l)\) rule: the lower \(n + l\) is lower in energy, and for equal \(n + l\) the one with the lower \(n\) is lower.

| # | \(n\) | \(l\) | Orbital | \(n + l\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 2 | \(4d\) | 6 |
| 2 | 3 | 2 | \(3d\) | 5 |
| 3 | 4 | 1 | \(4p\) | 5 |
| 4 | 3 | 2 | \(3d\) | 5 |
| 5 | 3 | 1 | \(3p\) | 4 |
| 6 | 4 | 1 | \(4p\) | 5 |

Electron 5 has the smallest \(n + l\). Electrons 2, 3, 4 and 6 all have \(n + l = 5\); of these, 2 and 4 have the lower \(n\) (3) so they lie below 3 and 6 (\(n = 4\)). Electron 1 has the largest \(n + l\).

Answer, in increasing order of energy:

\(5 < 2 = 4 < 3 = 6 < 1\)

Same-energy combinations: 2 and 4 (both \(3d\)), and 3 and 6 (both \(4p\)) — they differ only in \(m_l\) or \(m_s\), which do not affect the energy in a free atom.

The effective nuclear charge \(Z_{\text{eff}}\) felt by an electron is the actual nuclear charge reduced by the screening of the electrons between it and the nucleus. The further out the shell, the more inner electrons lie between it and the nucleus, and the more it is screened.

In bromine (\(Z = 35\), \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^2\,4p^5\)) the three sets named lie in shells \(n = 2\), \(n = 3\) and \(n = 4\). The \(4p\) electrons are the outermost, screened by every one of the 28 electrons inside them, whereas the \(2p\) electrons are screened only by the two \(1s\) electrons.

Answer: the electrons in the \(4p\) orbital experience the lowest effective nuclear charge.

Two effects decide \(Z_{\text{eff}}\): an orbital closer to the nucleus is screened by fewer electrons, and within a shell an orbital that penetrates closer to the nucleus (the order of penetration being \(s > p > d > f\)) feels the nucleus more strongly.

(i) \(2s\) and \(3s\): the \(2s\) orbital is nearer the nucleus and is screened by fewer inner electrons, so \(2s\) experiences the larger \(Z_{\text{eff}}\).

(ii) \(4d\) and \(4f\): same shell, so penetration decides it. A \(4d\) orbital penetrates closer to the nucleus than \(4f\), so \(4d\) experiences the larger \(Z_{\text{eff}}\).

(iii) \(3d\) and \(3p\): same shell again, and \(3p\) penetrates more than \(3d\), so \(3p\) experiences the larger \(Z_{\text{eff}}\).

Answer: (i) \(2s\); (ii) \(4d\); (iii) \(3p\).

Al has \(Z = 13\) with configuration \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^1\); Si has \(Z = 14\) with \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^2\).

The unpaired electrons are in \(3p\) in both, and both are screened by the same set of inner shells (\(1s\,2s\,2p\,3s\)). Electrons within the same subshell screen one another only weakly, so the extra \(3p\) electron in silicon does not offset its extra unit of nuclear charge.

Since silicon has one more proton with essentially the same screening, its \(3p\) electrons feel the greater pull.

Answer: the \(3p\) electrons of SILICON experience the more effective nuclear charge.

Write each configuration and apply Hund's rule (electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly before pairing).

(a) P (\(Z = 15\)): \([\text{Ne}]\,3s^2\,3p^3\) — three \(3p\) orbitals each singly filled: 3 unpaired.

(b) Si (\(Z = 14\)): \([\text{Ne}]\,3s^2\,3p^2\) — two \(3p\) orbitals singly filled: 2 unpaired.

(c) Cr (\(Z = 24\)): \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1\) (the half-filled \(3d\) is the more stable arrangement) — five singly-filled \(3d\) plus one \(4s\): 6 unpaired.

(d) Fe (\(Z = 26\)): \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^6\,4s^2\) — one \(3d\) orbital is paired and four are singly filled: 4 unpaired.

(e) Kr (\(Z = 36\)): \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^2\,4p^6\) — every orbital is filled: 0 unpaired.

Answer: (a) 3, (b) 2, (c) 6, (d) 4, (e) 0.

(a) For a given \(n\), the azimuthal quantum number takes the values \(l = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1\), and each value of \(l\) is one subshell. So the number of subshells equals \(n\).

For \(n = 4\): \(l = 0, 1, 2, 3\), i.e. the \(4s\), \(4p\), \(4d\) and \(4f\) subshells — 4 subshells.

(b) The shell \(n = 4\) holds \(2n^2 = 32\) electrons in all. Each orbital takes one electron with \(m_s = +\tfrac{1}{2}\) and one with \(m_s = -\tfrac{1}{2}\), so exactly half of them have \(m_s = -\tfrac{1}{2}\).

\(\dfrac{32}{2} = 16\)

Answer: (a) 4 subshells; (b) 16 electrons.
